cda-childcare-readiness-check-safe-healt.prompt: In a preschool classroom, which two times require handwashing for both the children and the teaching staff?

options.a: Before eating and after using the toilet
options.b: Before going outdoors and before naptime
options.c: After circle time and after art with markers
options.d: Before table toys and after story time

cda-childcare-readiness-check-safe-healt.explanation: Handwashing with soap and running water is most important at the moments germs move from hands to mouths or from bodily waste to hands: on arrival, before and after eating or handling food, after toileting or diapering, after outdoor or sand play, and after wiping noses. Adults follow the same key times, and wearing gloves does not replace washing afterward.

distractorExplanations.b: Going outdoors and lying down for nap are not key handwashing points; washing is needed after outdoor play, not before it.
distractorExplanations.c: Circle time and marker art carry little germ risk, so these are not the times the health guidelines single out for handwashing.
distractorExplanations.d: Picking up table toys and listening to a story are low-risk transitions; the true key times are before eating and after toileting.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-safe-healt.prompt: An infant teacher puts on disposable gloves to change a soiled diaper. At which point in the change should she take the gloves off?

options.a: After she puts the child back down to play with the group
options.b: After the soiled diaper and wipes go into the lined can
options.c: After the clean diaper is on and the child is dressed
options.d: When the gloves become visibly soiled during the change

cda-childcare-readiness-check-safe-healt.explanation: Gloves are removed as soon as the dirty part of the change is finished: clean the child, put the soiled diaper and wipes in a lined, hands-free can, then take off the gloves. This keeps germs off the clean diaper, the child's clothes, and the room. The change ends with washing the child's hands, disinfecting the table, and washing the adult's hands.

distractorExplanations.a: Keeping soiled gloves on while carrying the child back to the group spreads germs from the changing table to the child and the classroom.
distractorExplanations.c: Putting on the clean diaper and clothes with contaminated gloves transfers stool germs onto the very items that should stay clean.
distractorExplanations.d: Gloves are contaminated by the diaper whether or not soil is visible, so removal is tied to the step in the sequence, not to how they look.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-safe-healt.prompt: Which crib setup follows safe sleep guidance for a healthy 4-month-old at naptime in a child care center?

options.a: Baby on her side, propped with a rolled towel behind her
options.b: Baby on her back, under a light blanket tucked at the chest
options.c: Baby on her back on a firm mattress with only a fitted sheet
options.d: Baby on her tummy if that is how she sleeps best at home

cda-childcare-readiness-check-safe-healt.explanation: Current AAP and Caring for Our Children guidance is to place every infant on the back for every sleep, on a firm, flat mattress covered by a tight fitted sheet, with no blankets, pillows, bumpers, or toys in the crib. Soft items and non-back positions raise the risk of SIDS and suffocation.

distractorExplanations.a: Side sleeping is outdated advice; babies can roll from the side onto the tummy, and a rolled towel is a soft item that should not be in the crib.
distractorExplanations.b: Tucking a light blanket was once recommended, but any loose bedding can cover the baby's face; a wearable sleep sack is the safe option.
distractorExplanations.d: Tummy sleeping at home does not change the rule; a different position in care requires a written medical waiver from the child's doctor.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-safe-healt.prompt: A family child care provider is serving lunch to a mixed-age group that includes an 18-month-old. Which way of serving food is safest for the toddler?

options.a: Slice the hot dogs into thin, round coins
options.b: Serve whole grapes, since they are soft
options.c: Offer popcorn instead of raw carrot sticks
options.d: Cut the grapes lengthwise into quarters

cda-childcare-readiness-check-safe-healt.explanation: Children under 3 have small airways, so round, firm foods that can plug the throat are cut into small pieces before serving. Grapes and cherry tomatoes are quartered lengthwise, hot dogs are cut lengthwise and then into small bits, and hard snacks like popcorn, nuts, and raw carrots are avoided. The same idea applies to toys: objects small enough to fit in a choke tube are kept away from under-3s.

distractorExplanations.a: Round coins keep the hot dog's circular shape, which can still seal a toddler's airway; hot dogs must be cut lengthwise first.
distractorExplanations.b: Softness does not prevent choking; a whole grape is the right size and shape to block a toddler's windpipe.
distractorExplanations.c: Popcorn is itself a listed choking hazard for children under 3, so swapping it for raw carrots trades one hazard for another.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-safe-healt.prompt: Leo, age 3, has a peanut allergy action plan and an epinephrine auto-injector at the center. A parent brings store-bought cookies for a birthday. What should the teacher do?

options.a: Read the label for peanut and "may contain" warnings first
options.b: Ask Leo if peanuts make him sick before giving him a cookie
options.c: Serve the cookies and keep his auto-injector locked in the office
options.d: Give Leo a cookie after picking off any visible nut pieces

cda-childcare-readiness-check-safe-healt.explanation: Managing a food allergy means preventing exposure and being ready to respond. Staff check every outside food label for the allergen and for "may contain" or shared-equipment warnings before serving it, follow the child's written action plan, and keep the epinephrine with or near the child and teachers trained to use it. If the label is unclear, the child gets a safe alternative snack.

distractorExplanations.b: A 3-year-old cannot reliably judge which foods contain peanuts; the decision rests with adults reading labels and following the plan.
distractorExplanations.c: A locked office delays epinephrine in an emergency; the auto-injector should travel with the child and be quickly reachable by staff.
distractorExplanations.d: Removing visible nuts does not remove peanut protein from the cookie, so cross-contact can still cause a serious reaction.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-safe-healt.prompt: A parent drops off her son's prescribed antibiotic and asks the teacher to give the noon dose. What does the teacher need before giving it?

options.a: The parent's verbal OK and the child's weight to check the dose chart
options.b: Signed parent permission and the original pharmacy-labeled bottle
options.c: A handwritten note and the dose poured into a labeled cup
options.d: The director's approval and a kitchen spoon to measure it

cda-childcare-readiness-check-safe-healt.explanation: Programs give medicine only with written, signed permission from the parent and only from the original container labeled with the child's name, the medicine, the dose, and the time. Staff measure with a proper dosing tool and record each dose in the medication log, which prevents wrong-child, wrong-dose, and double-dose errors.

distractorExplanations.a: A verbal OK leaves no written record, and staff do not work out doses from a chart; the dose comes from the prescription label.
distractorExplanations.c: Medicine moved into another container loses the pharmacy label, so staff cannot confirm the drug, the child's name, or the correct dose.
distractorExplanations.d: The director cannot replace the parent's written permission, and kitchen spoons vary in size, which leads to under- or overdosing.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-safe-healt.prompt: A toddler room has a diaper-changing table and a bin of toys that children often put in their mouths. Which cleaning plan matches current health guidance?

options.a: Diaper table: sanitize after each use; mouthed toys: disinfect them weekly
options.b: Diaper table: spray disinfectant; mouthed toys: rinse them in water
options.c: Diaper table: clean, then disinfect; mouthed toys: clean, then sanitize
options.d: Diaper table: wipe with soapy water; mouthed toys: spray disinfectant

cda-childcare-readiness-check-safe-healt.explanation: Cleaning with soap and water removes dirt so the chemical step can work. Diaper tables and other surfaces exposed to body fluids need the stronger step, disinfecting, after every change. Toys that go in mouths are cleaned and then sanitized, a gentler level that reduces germs and is safe for items children mouth; they are pulled out after each child mouths them.

distractorExplanations.a: This swaps the two levels: the diaper table needs disinfecting, and weekly disinfectant on mouthed toys is both too infrequent and too harsh.
distractorExplanations.b: Spraying disinfectant on a dirty table skips the cleaning step that lets it work, and a water rinse does not sanitize mouthed toys.
distractorExplanations.d: Soapy water alone cleans but does not kill the germs on a diaper table, and full-strength disinfectant is meant for surfaces, not mouthed toys.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-safe-healt.prompt: A teacher in an infant room cares for four babies who cannot walk yet. During a fire drill, how should she get them out of the building?

options.a: Carry one baby out at a time and come back in for the next
options.b: Keep the babies in their cribs and wait for the firefighters
options.c: Gather the babies' bottles and bags first, then carry them out
options.d: Place them in an evacuation crib and roll it to the exit

cda-childcare-readiness-check-safe-healt.explanation: Infant rooms keep an evacuation crib or multi-seat buggy near the exit so non-walking babies can leave together in one trip. Drills are practiced on the schedule licensing requires so staff and children know the route, the meeting spot, and the head count, and the teacher takes the attendance list and emergency contacts, not personal belongings.

distractorExplanations.a: Going back into a burning building for each baby wastes critical time and puts the teacher and the remaining infants at risk.
distractorExplanations.b: Waiting in place is for shelter-in-place events like severe weather; a fire requires everyone to leave the building right away.
distractorExplanations.c: Stopping to collect bottles and bags delays the evacuation; only the attendance record and emergency contact information go out.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-safe-healt.prompt: Preschoolers are coming in from the playground to wash up for lunch. Which approach shows active supervision during this transition?

options.a: Count children as they line up and again once they are inside
options.b: Lead the line inside and trust the assistant to bring stragglers
options.c: Stand at the sink with her back to the room to help with washing
options.d: Ask the oldest children to check that no one is left outside

cda-childcare-readiness-check-safe-healt.explanation: Transitions are when children are most often left behind or wander off. Active supervision means counting children before and after every move, placing adults so they can see and hear the whole group, scanning constantly, and anticipating where problems may happen. A name-to-face count against attendance confirms everyone made it inside.

distractorExplanations.b: Assuming another adult will collect stragglers is how children get left outside; each teacher confirms the count herself.
distractorExplanations.c: Helping at the sink is fine, but standing with her back to the room means she cannot see or hear the rest of the group.
distractorExplanations.d: Supervision is an adult responsibility; preschoolers cannot be relied on to account for every child in the group.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-safe-healt.prompt: A family child care provider is installing a new climber in her backyard play area. What should she put under and around it?

options.a: Packed dirt that has been raked smooth
options.b: A deep layer of wood chips or rubber mulch
options.c: Thick green grass that is mowed short
options.d: Outdoor carpet laid over the concrete patio

cda-childcare-readiness-check-safe-healt.explanation: Falls from equipment are the leading cause of playground injuries, so climbers need loose-fill or rubber surfacing deep enough to cushion a fall, covering the whole fall zone that extends at least 6 feet out from the equipment. Providers also check the surface daily, rake loose fill back into place, and watch for sun, heat, and hot slides.

distractorExplanations.a: Packed dirt is hard enough to cause head injuries in a fall; raking the top does not give it any cushioning depth.
distractorExplanations.c: Grass looks soft, but the ground beneath it compacts and does not absorb the impact of a fall from climbing height.
distractorExplanations.d: Thin outdoor carpet over concrete gives almost no shock absorption, so a child who falls still lands on a hard surface.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-safe-healt.prompt: A preschool teacher is planning afternoon snack and wants it to support healthy growth. Which menu is the best choice?

options.a: Fruit-flavored yogurt tubes and juice boxes
options.b: Granola bars and a cup of 100% apple juice
options.c: Apple slices, cheese cubes, and water
options.d: Whole-grain crackers and a fruit punch drink

cda-childcare-readiness-check-safe-healt.explanation: A nutritious snack pairs at least two food groups, such as a whole fruit or vegetable with a protein or dairy food, and offers water to drink. Whole fruit gives fiber that juice lacks, and water keeps children hydrated without added sugar, which is why programs limit juice and avoid sweetened drinks.

distractorExplanations.a: Flavored yogurt tubes and juice boxes both carry a lot of added or concentrated sugar, so the snack is high in sugar and low in fiber.
distractorExplanations.b: Granola bars are often sweetened, and 100% juice still lacks the fiber of whole fruit, so the snack falls short of a balanced choice.
distractorExplanations.d: Whole-grain crackers are a good start, but fruit punch is a sugary drink that adds empty calories instead of hydration.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-safe-healt.prompt: An infant teacher is getting a bottle of a mother's expressed breast milk ready for a hungry 5-month-old. Which practice is safe?

options.a: Heat it in the microwave for a few seconds and swirl it well
options.b: Prop the bottle on a rolled blanket so the baby can feed in the crib
options.c: Dip the nipple in a little honey to encourage a fussy baby to eat
options.d: Warm it in a cup of warm water and hold the baby to feed

cda-childcare-readiness-check-safe-healt.explanation: Bottles are warmed in warm water or a bottle warmer, checked for temperature, and given while the caregiver holds the baby. Holding the infant prevents choking, supports bonding, and lets the adult follow hunger cues. Staff also label milk with the child's name, follow the family's feeding instructions, and avoid honey before 12 months.

distractorExplanations.a: Microwaves heat unevenly and create hot spots that can burn a baby's mouth even after swirling, so they are not used for bottles.
distractorExplanations.b: A propped bottle keeps milk flowing even if the baby cannot swallow, which risks choking and ear infections and removes adult contact.
distractorExplanations.c: Honey can carry spores that cause infant botulism, so it is not given in any amount to babies younger than 12 months.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-safe-healt.prompt: At 10 a.m., a toddler who was fine at drop-off becomes flushed, cries, and refuses to play. A temperature check shows a fever. What should the teacher do first?

options.a: Move him to a quiet, supervised spot and call his family
options.b: Give him a fever reducer from the first-aid kit and watch him
options.c: Let him rest on a cot in the nap room alone until pickup time
options.d: Keep him with the group and mention the fever to his family at pickup

cda-childcare-readiness-check-safe-healt.explanation: A child with a fever who also cannot take part in normal activities meets common exclusion criteria. The teacher separates him from the group while keeping him in sight, contacts the family to pick him up, and documents the symptoms. The program's health policy, not the teacher's guess, decides when he may return.

distractorExplanations.b: Staff cannot give any medicine, including fever reducers, without written parent permission, and lowering the fever does not end the illness.
distractorExplanations.c: Separating an ill child is right, but leaving a toddler alone in another room is unsafe; he must remain within an adult's sight.
distractorExplanations.d: Waiting until pickup leaves a sick child in group care, exposes the others, and keeps the family uninformed when they need to act.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-safe-healt.prompt: A preschool teacher is rearranging her classroom learning centers. Where should she place the block area?

options.a: Next to the book corner, so children can build stories with blocks
options.b: Away from the book corner, near other active, noisy centers
options.c: In the middle of the room, so the main walkway passes through it
options.d: In a back corner behind tall shelves, so towers are not knocked over

cda-childcare-readiness-check-safe-healt.explanation: Room arrangement groups noisy, active centers like blocks and dramatic play together and keeps quiet centers like books and writing on the other side. Centers have clear boundaries, walkways go around them rather than through them, shelves are low enough for adults to see the whole room, and materials sit on labeled, child-height shelves.

distractorExplanations.a: Linking blocks and books is a good idea for activities, but placing them side by side lets building noise disrupt children who are reading.
distractorExplanations.c: A walkway through the block area leads to knocked-over structures and collisions; traffic paths should go around play spaces.
distractorExplanations.d: Tall shelves that hide a corner block the teacher's line of sight, so she cannot supervise children working in that area.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-safe-healt.prompt: A new lead teacher is drafting the daily schedule for her full-day preschool class. Which plan reflects best practice?

options.a: Long whole-group lessons each morning, with free play saved for after nap
options.b: A different order of activities each day so children stay curious
options.c: Active and quiet times that alternate, with outdoor play and free choice
options.d: Mostly teacher-led activities so each part of the day has a set goal

cda-childcare-readiness-check-safe-healt.explanation: A strong preschool schedule balances active and quiet periods, indoor and outdoor play, and child-chosen and teacher-led activities, and it follows the same order each day. Long free-choice blocks and short group times match preschoolers' attention spans, and a predictable routine helps children feel secure and handle transitions.

distractorExplanations.a: Long whole-group lessons exceed preschoolers' attention spans, and pushing free play to the afternoon removes child-chosen learning from the morning.
distractorExplanations.b: Changing the order every day makes the routine unpredictable, which increases anxiety and behavior problems during transitions.
distractorExplanations.d: A schedule built mostly on teacher-led activities leaves too little time for child-chosen play, where much preschool learning happens.
